content: The pubic louse, also known as the crab louse (Pthirus pubis), is a parasitic insect that resides exclusively on human hair and feeds solely on human blood throughout its life cycle. Humans are the only known host for this parasite. In addition to pubic lice, humans can also be infested with body lice (Pediculus humanus humanus) and head lice (Pediculus humanus capitis). The body of the pubic louse is dorsoventrally flattened and divided into three distinct regions: the head, thorax, and abdomen. The head features a pair of eyes and a pair of antennae, which are clearly visible. The mouthparts are specialized for piercing the skin and extracting blood. The second and third pairs of legs are equipped with terminal claws that are adapted for gripping hair shafts, while the first pair of legs is used to hold onto the skin during feeding. The abdomen has characteristic lateral protuberances that are unique to this species. Male lice are slightly smaller than females. The eggs, or nits, are oval-shaped and approximately 0.8 mm in length. Immediately after being laid, the eggs appear shiny, round, and transparent. Adult pubic lice measure between 1 and 2 mm in size, depending on their developmental stage. They are typically whitish-gray in color but may turn reddish-brown temporarily after consuming a blood meal. Pubic lice are obligate insect parasites that spend their entire life on the host's hair and skin, feeding exclusively on blood up to 4–5 times daily. Their life cycle, from egg to adult, spans 22–27 days. The eggs hatch into the first nymphal stage, which undergoes three successive molts to develop into the second and third nymphal stages before maturing into either an adult male or female louse. The incubation period for the eggs is 7–8 days, with the remainder of the life cycle dedicated to the development of the nymphal stages. On average, adult female lice live for 17 days, while males live for approximately 22 days. Genetic research suggests that pubic lice are closely related to the louse species endemic to gorillas, Pthirus gorillae. It is believed that pubic lice were transmitted to early hominids from the ancestors of gorillas several million years ago. This theory contrasts with the previously held belief that pubic lice diverged from human head lice.
